title: No-Fault vs At-Fault Car Insurance States: Which One Is Yours and Who Pays After a Crash?
description: No-fault vs at-fault car insurance states explained: the full list of no-fault states, how PIP and tort thresholds work, and who pays your bills after a crash.
author: Insurance Bhaiya Research Desk
keyTakeaways: Twelve states use no-fault car insurance: Florida, Hawaii, Kansas, Kentucky, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New York, North Dakota, Pennsylvania and Utah. The rest, including [Texas](/qa/is-texas-a-no-fault-state/), [Georgia](/qa/is-georgia-a-no-fault-state/) and [Colorado](/qa/is-colorado-a-no-fault-state/), are at-fault (tort) states.

In a no-fault state, your own [personal injury protection](/glossary/personal-injury-protection/) pays your medical bills first, whoever caused the crash. In an at-fault state, the driver who caused it (through their liability insurance) pays.
No-fault only covers injuries. Car damage is still decided by fault in every state.

You can step outside no-fault and sue only when your injuries pass a [tort threshold](/glossary/tort-threshold/). In New York that means a 'serious injury' as defined in law. See [New York no-fault insurance](/learn/new-york-no-fault-insurance/).

About 1 in 3 US drivers were uninsured or underinsured in 2023 ([IRC](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20250220231032/en/One-in-Three-US-Drivers-Are-Either-Uninsured-or-Underinsured-Exposing-Themselves-and-Other-Drivers-to-Significant-Financial-Risk-New-IRC-Study-Shows)). In an at-fault state, that makes your own uninsured motorist coverage your safety net. See [is uninsured motorist coverage required in Georgia](/qa/is-uninsured-motorist-coverage-required-in-georgia/).

faqs.question: Which states are no-fault states?
faqs.answer: Florida, Hawaii, Kansas, Kentucky, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New York, North Dakota, Pennsylvania and Utah. Kentucky, New Jersey and Pennsylvania are 'choice' no-fault states, where you can pay more to keep full rights to sue.

faqs.question: Is no-fault insurance better than at-fault?
faqs.answer: Neither is simply better. No-fault pays injury bills faster and reduces small lawsuits, but limits your right to sue and tends to cost more. At-fault systems keep full lawsuit rights but can leave you waiting, or unpaid, if the other driver is uninsured or blame is disputed.

faqs.question: Does no-fault insurance cover car damage?
faqs.answer: No. No-fault (PIP) covers injuries. Vehicle damage is paid by the at-fault driver's property damage liability or your own collision coverage, in every state.

faqs.question: Can I sue in a no-fault state?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your injury meets the state's tort threshold (for example, New York's 'serious injury' categories), or for vehicle damage. See [tort threshold](/glossary/tort-threshold/).

faqs.question: If I'm in a crash in another state, whose rules apply?
faqs.answer: Generally the law of the state where the crash happened decides fault and lawsuit rights, while your own policy's coverages, such as PIP, follow you. Most policies automatically adjust to meet another state's minimums while you drive there. Our [Texas driver in New York scenario](/scenarios/texas-driver-crash-in-new-york-no-fault) walks through a real example.

content.text: Picture two crashes that are exactly alike. A driver runs a red light and T-bones you, and you walk away with a broken wrist and $9,000 in medical bills. In Houston you'd claim against the other driver's insurance and wait while fault gets sorted out. In Brooklyn you'd file with your own insurer within 30 days, and it would start paying your bills whoever was to blame. Same crash, very different process. That's the difference between **at-fault and no-fault car insurance states**, and it shapes what coverage you should buy, how fast you get paid and whether you can sue.

This hub explains both systems in plain English, lists every no-fault state, and links to state-by-state answers. If you're new to car insurance, start with our [car insurance guide](/learn/car-insurance-guide/) and [car insurance basics](/learn/car-insurance-basics-registration-cost-claims/), then come back here.

In a **no-fault state**, every driver must carry [personal injury protection (PIP)](/glossary/personal-injury-protection/). After a crash, your own PIP pays your medical bills, and usually some lost wages, no matter who caused it. Your passengers generally claim on your PIP too, and pedestrians you hit may be covered under it. The trade-off is that your right to sue the other driver for pain and suffering is limited. You can only sue when your injuries pass the state's [tort threshold](/glossary/tort-threshold/). The idea is faster payment for everyday injuries and fewer lawsuits over minor ones.

In an **at-fault state**, the person who caused the crash is financially responsible, and so is their bodily injury liability insurance. You claim against the at-fault driver's insurer, or sue them, for medical bills, lost wages, pain and suffering and car damage. There's no threshold, so you can sue for any injury. The catch is that payment waits until fault is established, and if you were partly to blame, your payout may be cut or wiped out under your state's comparative negligence rule. That's why at-fault states lean on optional coverages such as [MedPay and PIP](/compare/pip-vs-medpay) and uninsured motorist coverage to fill the gap.

content.title: No-Fault Doesn't Mean No Blame
content.text: This is the most common misunderstanding. No-fault only changes who pays for **injuries** first. Car damage is still decided by fault in every state: the at-fault driver's property damage liability pays for your car, or your own [collision coverage](/compare/comprehensive-vs-collision/) does. Fault also still goes on the at-fault driver's record and can raise their premium. See [how long an accident stays on your insurance](/qa/how-long-does-an-accident-stay-on-your-insurance/).

content.text: Comparative Fault: How Blame Gets Split in At-Fault States

Most crashes aren't 100/0. States split blame under [comparative negligence](/glossary/comparative-negligence/) rules in one of three ways, and it decides whether you get paid at all. According to [Bloomberg Law's state-by-state negligence chart](https://pro.bloomberglaw.com/insights/litigation/contributory-and-comparative-negligence-by-state/):

items: **Modified comparative, 51% bar.** You recover damages reduced by your share of fault, but nothing if you're 51% or more to blame. Texas uses this rule. See [is Texas an at-fault state](/qa/is-texas-a-no-fault-state/).

**Modified comparative, 50% bar.** You recover nothing at 50% or more. Georgia and Colorado use versions of this rule. See [is Georgia a no-fault state](/qa/is-georgia-a-no-fault-state/) and [is Colorado a no-fault state](/qa/is-colorado-a-no-fault-state/).
**Pure comparative.** You recover something even if you're mostly at fault, reduced by your share. New York uses this rule for lawsuits that clear its no-fault threshold.
**Contributory negligence.** A handful of places bar recovery if you're even 1% at fault.

content.title: Be Careful What You Say to the Other Driver's Insurer
content.text: In at-fault states, adjusters use recorded statements to assign percentages of blame. A casual 'I didn't see him' can cost you 20% of your claim. Read [can I refuse a recorded statement to an insurance company](/qa/can-i-refuse-a-recorded-statement-to-insurance-company/) before you call them back.

The [Insurance Research Council](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20250220231032/en/One-in-Three-US-Drivers-Are-Either-Uninsured-or-Underinsured-Exposing-Themselves-and-Other-Drivers-to-Significant-Financial-Risk-New-IRC-Study-Shows) estimates that 15.4% of US drivers were uninsured in 2023 and 33.4% were either uninsured or underinsured. In an at-fault state, if the driver who hit you has no insurance, there's no liability policy to claim against. Your own **uninsured/underinsured motorist (UM/UIM)** coverage steps in. Some states require it, and others require insurers to include it unless you reject it in writing. Georgia is a good example, covered in [is uninsured motorist coverage required in Georgia](/qa/is-uninsured-motorist-coverage-required-in-georgia/) and in our real-life [Atlanta uninsured driver scenario](/scenarios/uninsured-driver-crash-georgia-um-claim). For the legal side, see [can an insurance company sue an uninsured driver](/qa/can-an-insurance-company-sue-an-uninsured-driver/).
What Coverage Should You Buy in Each System?

items: **In a no-fault state:** Buy more than the minimum PIP if you can. New York's $50,000 goes fast after surgery. Carry solid bodily injury limits anyway, because serious crashes still end up in court. Learn the claim steps in [how to file a no-fault insurance claim in New York](/qa/how-to-file-a-no-fault-insurance-claim-in-new-york/).

**In an at-fault state:** Don't decline MedPay or PIP when your insurer offers it. It pays while fault is argued over. Compare the two in [PIP vs MedPay](/compare/pip-vs-medpay). Colorado insurers must include $5,000 of MedPay unless you reject it in writing.

**Everywhere:** Carry UM/UIM matching your liability limits, liability of at least 100/300/100 if you have assets to protect, and an [umbrella policy](/learn/umbrella-insurance-guide/) once your net worth exceeds those limits. Check yourself with [how to know if you are underinsured](/learn/how-to-know-if-you-are-underinsured/).
